sentences.text: ORDER A common question arises in all these cases.
The petitioner is a Devaswom and were supplemental claimants in the land acquisition references relating to acquisition of lands for the purpose of National Highway.
According to them, they were the 'jenmis' of the lands which have been acquired and the original claimants were tenants under them.
They claimed entitlement to the compensation awarded.
The Reference Court negatived the contentions of the petitioner and that has led to the filing of these Civil Revision Petitions.

The grounds raised in the Civil Revision Petitions are that the leases in favour of the original claimants are all hit by Section 29 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, that the certificates of purchase issued by the Land Tribunal in favour of the original claimants cannot be relied upon as CRP NO. 458 OF 2025 & con.cases 2026:KER:29055 conclusive proof of their title, that the properties are exempted under Section 3(1)(x) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act from the provisions of the Act and hence it should be treated as belonging to the Devaswom, and that the certificates of purchase were issued without compliance with the Kerala Land Reforms (Vesting and Assignment) Rules, 1970.

entities.label: STATUTE

entities.text: Kerala Land Reforms (Vesting and Assignment) Rules, 1970
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text:
There is also a contention that the lease cannot be justified in view of Section 76 of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act,
1927.
2. The Reference Court has considered all the above arguments.

Regarding the contention that the lease was not valid in view of Section 76 (1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927,
the Court held that the leases were even prior to the Act and hence the provision will not apply.
Moreover, the Act was repealed by Section 5 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 and it was notified in Kerala in 1956 by virtue of Kerala Adaption of Laws Order, 1956.

entities.text: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The provision relied on was never given a retrospective effect, to take away the right of the tenants who were in possession even prior to the coming into force of the Act.
I do not find any reason to interfere with the said finding CRP NO. 458 OF 2025 & con.cases 2026:KER:29055 of the Reference Court.

As regards the validity of the certificates of purchase, the said contention also cannot be raised at this point of time, particularly since there is no effective challenge to the certificates of purchase.
It is only in LAR 31 of 2024, from which CRP(LR) No.33 of 2025 arises, that it is submitted, an appeal has been filed with a delay.
The pendency of an appeal need not stop this case from being decided.
The challenge on the ground of validity of the purchase certificate also cannot be countenanced, particularly since the tenants were in possession from prior to 1927.
The next argument is based on Section 3(1)(x) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act.

According to the counsel for the petitioner, the Land Reforms Act cannot apply to tenancies in respect of sites, tanks and premises of any temple on which religious ceremonies are conducted and sites of office buildings and other buildings attached to such temple.

The Reference Court found that none of the lands in question can be treated as premises of a temple where religious ceremonies are conducted or where buildings attached to the temple have been constructed.

The Court found that these were lands CRP Chirakkal Kovilakam Devaswoms vs The Special Tahsildar on 31 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/25532192/
18 NO. 458 OF 2025 & con.cases 2026:KER:29055 which were leased out for conducting cultivation.

sentences.text: In view of the specific finding on the fact, the contention based on Section 3(1)(x) is not sustainable.

None of the grounds raised are sufficient to dislodge the finding of the Additional District Court-II,
Thalassery.
3. The Civil Revision Petitions fail and are dismissed.
This Court is not expressing any view regarding the appeal which is stated to be pending against the purchase certificate which had been issued to the claimant under LAR 31 of 2024.

opennyai_summary.facts:
The petitioner is a Devaswom and were supplemental claimants in the land acquisition references relating to acquisition of lands for the purpose of National Highway.
They claimed entitlement to the compensation awarded.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
The grounds raised in the Civil Revision Petitions are that the leases in favour of the original claimants are all hit by Section 29 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, that the certificates of purchase issued by the Land Tribunal in favour of the original claimants cannot be relied upon as CRP NO. 458 OF 2025 & con.cases 2026:KER:29055 conclusive proof of their title, that the properties are exempted under Section 3(1)(x) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act from the provisions of the Act and hence it should be treated as belonging to the Devaswom, and that the certificates of purchase were issued without compliance with the Kerala Land Reforms (Vesting and Assignment) Rules, 1970.
There is also a contention that the lease cannot be justified in view of Section 76 of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act,
1927.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Moreover, the Act was repealed by Section 5 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 and it was notified in Kerala in 1956 by virtue of Kerala Adaption of Laws Order, 1956.
The provision relied on was never given a retrospective effect, to take away the right of the tenants who were in possession even prior to the coming into force of the Act.
The pendency of an appeal need not stop this case from being decided.
The Reference Court found that none of the lands in question can be treated as premises of a temple where religious ceremonies are conducted or where buildings attached to the temple have been constructed.
